content: 1. Studies suggest that individuals who harbor colonizing pathogens may transmit these resistant organisms to other members of their household. For example, a study conducted in Tanzania observed high rates of azithromycin resistance in nasopharyngeal isolates of Streptococcus pneumoniae and Staphylococcus aureus among children in a district where mass drug administration (MDA) had ceased four years prior. This finding implies potential transmission of resistant strains within households. However, due to the lack of pre-treatment resistance data, this conclusion remains speculative. 2. No studies have specifically investigated antibiotic resistance (other than macrolide-related resistance) in respiratory bacteria among household contacts of children treated with MDA-azithromycin. 3. The World Health Organization (WHO) has recognized the clear benefits of mass azithromycin treatments for endemic diseases, such as trachoma, where it has significantly reduced the prevalence of ocular Chlamydia strains and, in some areas, may have led to the elimination of infection. However, the adverse effects of such mass treatments are less well understood. 4. Some studies have reported significant increases in macrolide resistance in fecal and nasopharyngeal bacteria following regular MDA-azithromycin. However, these studies often assume that MDA will be discontinued within a relatively short timeframe. In such cases, macrolide resistance, particularly in Streptococcus pneumoniae, may revert to baseline levels. It remains uncertain whether prolonged MDA programs aimed at improving childhood mortality outcomes could lead to sustained resistance thresholds, potentially facilitating the circulation of resistant strains. 5. The clinical impact of circulating resistant strains, particularly on enteric pathogens, cannot be determined with the currently available data. Future studies should adopt a standardized approach to monitor emerging resistance and detect unintended consequences. 6. Given that azithromycin is administered at the community level, resistance surveillance should aim to collect repeated cross-sectional data on colonizing bacteria across exposed communities, including both children and adults, rather than focusing solely on exposed children. Target bacteria of interest include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, Shigella spp., Escherichia coli, and Klebsiella spp., as these are key human pathogens. Resistance mechanisms in these bacteria may compromise the efficacy of Access category antibiotics listed in the WHO Essential Medicines List for treating severe bacterial infections. 7. In addition to community-based surveillance, it is important to track changes in the resistance of pathogenic organisms in children with severe illnesses who present to health facilities in exposed areas. This will help identify any adverse clinical effects associated with MDA-azithromycin. 8. A comprehensive literature search was conducted across multiple databases, including MEDLINE, PubMed, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Embase, CINAHL, and International Pharmaceutical Abstracts, to evaluate the safety of azithromycin. The search spanned from the inception of these databases to October 2018 and included studies in all languages. Adverse drug reaction (ADR) reporting systems and safety communication announcements were also reviewed. 9. The search strategy combined medical subject headings and free-text terms such as azithromycin and children. Inclusion criteria encompassed infants, toddlers, children, and adolescents aged 1 month to 18 years, with or without disease conditions. Studies enrolling only newborns (0–28 days) were excluded. 10. Patients were categorized into three age groups: infants and toddlers (28 days to 23 months), children (2 to 11 years), and adolescents (12 to 18 years). The daily dosage of azithromycin was divided into four groups: <10 mg/kg, 10–20 mg/kg, 20–30 mg/kg, and ≥30 mg/kg, based on WHO and British National Formulary guidelines. 11. A total of 118 articles on azithromycin safety were identified, including 78 randomized controlled trials (RCTs), 20 prospective cohort studies, seven retrospective cohort studies, 11 case reports, and two pharmacokinetic studies. These studies collectively involved 146,102 patients aged 1 month to 18 years. 12. Among the 78 RCTs, 72 evaluated the effectiveness and safety of azithromycin for treating infectious diseases or symptoms, while three specifically assessed the safety and effectiveness of MDA-azithromycin. Two RCTs compared annual treatment (a single oral dose of 20 mg/kg) with biannual treatment (a single oral dose every six months). Another RCT compared biannual MDA-azithromycin with placebo. 13. Gastrointestinal adverse events (AEs), such as diarrhea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and nausea, were the most commonly reported side effects in non-MDA-azithromycin studies. However, AEs were inadequately reported in MDA-azithromycin studies. For example, the MORDOR study reported 11 serious AEs among 97,047 children, including cases of malaria, respiratory infection, ileus, coma, and deaths. 14. Cardiac toxicity was rarely evaluated in children. One study in Egypt reported prolonged QT intervals in 82% of children receiving azithromycin weekly for six months, but the criteria for diagnosing QT prolongation were not provided. Another study in children with acute-onset neuropsychiatric syndrome reported borderline QTc intervals and elevated heart rates in some participants. 15. A retrospective cohort study found an increased risk of idiopathic hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (IHPS) in infants who received azithromycin during the first 90 days of life compared to those who did not receive macrolides. 16. The mode of action of azithromycin in reducing child mortality remains unclear. No studies have specifically investigated its mechanism of action in relation to individual infectious diseases. 17. The WHO recommends against the universal implementation of MDA-azithromycin for preventing childhood mortality due to low-quality evidence. However, it conditionally recommends MDA-azithromycin for children aged 1 to 11 months in sub-Saharan African settings with high infant and under-five mortality rates, provided that mortality rates, adverse effects, and antibiotic resistance are continuously monitored. 18. The suggested MDA-azithromycin regimen is 20 mg/kg as a single oral dose every six months. Further research is needed to determine the optimal dose, frequency, and number of intervention cycles. 19. Local consultation to confirm acceptability and preferences is essential when planning MDA-azithromycin implementation. Pharmacovigilance is particularly important in children under six months of age, as safety and efficacy data for this age group are limited. 20. In settings with low coverage of seasonal malaria chemoprophylaxis (SMC), scaling up SMC should take precedence over MDA-azithromycin implementation.
